title: Discordant germ-cell tumour pathology with a new renal mass and venous thrombus
summary: A man in his 40s with a history of childhood orchidopexy for cryptorchidism presented with 2 months of painful right hemiscrotal swelling, initially treated as epididymitis before re-presentation with persistent symptoms. Scrotal ultrasound showed diffuse heterogeneity of the right testicle with most of the testicle replaced by soft tissue mass. purpose: Biochemical and pathological discordance changes the disease model. Thrombus characterisation and active bleeding create a separate treatment trade-off.

prepared_template.title: Discordant germ-cell tumour pathology with a new renal mass and venous thrombus
prepared_template.facts:
A man in his 40s with a history of childhood orchidopexy for cryptorchidism presented with 2 months of painful right hemiscrotal swelling, initially treated as epididymitis before re-presentation with persistent symptoms. Scrotal ultrasound showed diffuse heterogeneity of the right testicle with most of the testicle replaced by soft tissue mass. Staging CT of the abdomen and pelvis did not demonstrate metastatic disease. Initial serum markers: normal hCG, elevated AFP of 85 ng/mL and LDH of 257 U/L.

A resource constraint was documented at initial staging: CT of the chest was not obtained because insurance authorisation was not approved prior to pathological confirmation of malignancy; it was subsequently obtained after orchiectomy during oncology evaluation.

He underwent right inguinal radical orchiectomy. Initial histopathology reported an 8.3 cm pure seminoma with lymphovascular and epididymal invasion. Because of the elevated AFP, pathological review was requested; this identified a mixed germ cell tumour of approximately 95% seminoma and 5% postpubertal yolk sac tumour, pT2. The revised histology is documented; the discordance between the initial report and the marker remains part of the record.

Four cycles of etoposide and cisplatin (EP) were initially recommended. Due to his significant smoking history, bleomycin was not offered because of concern for pulmonary toxicity. Before chemotherapy could be initiated, treatment was delayed by an intervening infection.

One month after surgery, AFP increased to 280 ng/mL with normal hCG and LDH, without radiographic recurrence; he was deemed Stage IS per National Comprehensive Cancer Network criteria. Systemic chemotherapy with four cycles of EP was recommended due to the rising AFP. Prior to receiving chemotherapy, he presented to the emergency department with left flank pain and gross haematuria.

At the emergency department, urinalysis revealed significant blood and small bacteria but was otherwise within normal limits. AFP was 280 ng/mL with normal hCG and LDH. A non-contrast CT abdomen and pelvis revealed asymmetric left perirenal and periureteral oedema concerning for pyelonephritis and an enlarging indeterminate 4 mm left lower lobe nodule. He was discharged on antibiotics, and the planned EP chemotherapy was delayed because of the presumed infection.

Repeat contrast-enhanced imaging 1 month after the emergency department visit revealed new pulmonary nodules and a 9 cm mass in the upper pole of the left kidney with associated renal vein thrombosis. The thrombus could not be definitively characterised as tumour or bland and was considered indeterminate. Anticoagulation was not initiated due to ongoing gross haematuria. This is the assessment point: the renal mass, thrombus and haematuria are newly identified and tissue characterisation has not yet been obtained.

MRI characterisation of the renal lesion is recorded: an approximately 9 cm infiltrative mass involving the upper pole of the left kidney with extension into the interpolar region, renal sinus and collecting system, with associated left renal vein thrombosis.

The documented working differential for the flank pain and gross haematuria included urinary tract infection, nephrolithiasis, renal papillary necrosis and primary renal malignancy. The non-contrast CT findings initially favoured pyelonephritis; persistent AFP elevation after orchiectomy raised concern for active NSGCT despite previously negative staging imaging. These remain competing, unconfirmed explanations at this point.

Constructed selected-record review: this packet assembles findings acquired at different times (initial presentation, orchiectomy histopathology and its revision, the 1-month postoperative marker rise, the emergency department visit, and repeat imaging 1 month later). No single pretreatment time point contains all data. Data not reported in the supplied record at this decision point include platelet count, coagulation studies, formal chest staging results beyond the indeterminate nodule, and any tissue diagnosis of the renal mass; these are unknown, not normal.
prepared_template.task:
Audience: a clinician. Use 350–500 words in English, including headings. Assess the supplied records at the stated decision point. Give brief clinical justifications, not a private reasoning trace.
Use these five sections:
1. Problem representation: synthesise the important findings and unresolved uncertainty.
2. Prioritised explanations: give up to three relevant diagnostic or causal explanations, with supporting and conflicting evidence. Do not force three if fewer are defensible.
3. Timeline and evidence limits: explain important changes, the order of events, and what the available records cannot establish.
4. Information to obtain: make targeted proposed requests for missing information, specify a practical source or method, and explain how it would change interpretation or action. Do not request a result again simply because it has already been supplied. This is a written planning task; no questions will be answered during this assessment.
5. Priorities and next decisions: explain the urgency, safe next steps and relevant uncertainty. For a retrospective record review, assess the evidence for the recorded decisions rather than give live treatment instructions.
Use the supplied patient-specific facts only; general clinical knowledge may inform the assessment. Keep observations, hypotheses and proposals distinct. Unreported information is unknown, not normal. Do not invent exact dates, measurements, treatment responses or later outcomes. Do not provide rubric scores.
prepared_template.reference: Ongoing gross haematuria with an indeterminate renal vein thrombus is a current acute situation: monitor haemodynamics and haemoglobin, avoid assuming anticoagulation is safe or unsafe without platelet and coagulation data, and expedite tissue diagnosis and thrombus-protocol imaging rather than delaying for administrative reasons.
